title: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution
learningObjectives: Deliver focused, flow-friendly care in the treatment area (MARCH priorities).
Set transport priorities and load vehicles efficiently.
Distribute patients across hospitals by capability and capacity.
Track every patient from tag to hospital bed.

summary.title: Treatment Area Care: Do What Changes Outcome
summary.content: MARCH: Massive hemorrhage (tourniquets, packing), Airway (position, adjuncts; advanced airways only if they don't stall flow), Respiration (seal open chest wounds, decompress tension pneumothorax, O2 to those who need it most), Circulation (bleeding control first; IV/IO and fluids selectively — permissive hypotension in penetrating trauma), Hypothermia/Head (keep everyone warm — blankets, ground insulation; protect the head-injured airway). Skip what doesn't change survival in the next hour: detailed secondary surveys, full spinal packaging of every patient, non-critical IVs. One provider can watch several yellows; reds need hands.

summary.title: Transport Priorities
summary.content: Reds first — especially those who need a surgeon now: non-compressible torso hemorrhage, airway that won't stay open, tension physiology not relieved, severe burns with airway involvement. Then yellows, then greens. Fill vehicles smartly: 1 red + 1–2 greens, or 2 yellows, per ambulance (per local policy and crew capacity). Move greens in bulk — buses or vans with a medic and a radio. Use air medical for long distances or specialty centers, but an LZ costs time — don't fly a patient a ground unit could have delivered sooner.

summary.title: Hospital Distribution: Distribute, Don't Dump
summary.content: The closest hospital gets hit first and hardest — often by walking wounded who self-present before EMS patients arrive ('upside-down triage': the first arrivals at hospital are the least injured). Send reds to the trauma center, burns to burn-capable centers, children to pediatric-capable hospitals when the time cost is acceptable, and spread yellows/greens to hospitals further out. Get capacity through one channel: the Medical Communications Coordinator / regional hospital coordination center (e.g., 'General can take 4 red, 8 yellow').

summary.title: Tracking: Every Patient Has a Trail
summary.content: Tag number → transport log → hospital. Without tracking, families can't find loved ones, hospitals can't anticipate, and patients 'disappear'. Log at the loading point (tag #, category, unit, destination, time). Hand the tear-off stub to the transport officer. Many systems use electronic patient tracking — scan the barcode on the tag. Family reunification centers depend on this data.

summary.title: Hospital Side (What EMS Should Know)
summary.content: Hospitals activate their own command system (e.g., HICS), clear ED beds, cancel elective surgery, and open surge areas. A classic CDC rule of thumb: roughly double the number of casualties arriving in the first hour to estimate the hospital's total. Expect decontamination at the hospital door for chemical incidents — many contaminated patients self-present. Give hospitals early, honest numbers so they can surge.

clinicalPearls: The fastest treatment in an MCI is often the ambulance door closing on a red patient headed to a surgeon.
Hypothermia is the silent MCI killer — insulate from the ground, not just on top.
Load reds with a green 'buddy' who can call for help if the red deteriorates — and fill empty seats.
First-hour hospital arrivals × 2 ≈ total expected at that hospital (rule of thumb).
If you can't remember where a patient went, nobody can. Log it.
redFlags: Treatment area turning into a field hospital with long procedures and no outflow.
All ambulances going to the closest hospital.
Patients leaving the scene without a log entry.
Greens self-evacuating in private cars untracked (they'll show up at the nearest ED).
commonMistakes: Intubating or starting multiple IVs on scene while transport units wait.
Not telling hospitals the real numbers early.
Forgetting pediatric/burn/trauma capability when assigning destinations.
memoryAids: MARCH: Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia/Head.
Vehicle math: 1 red + greens, 2 yellows, a busload of greens with a medic.

decisionTrees.title: Destination Decision
decisionTrees.content:
Patient ready for transport
  → RED?
     → Needs surgery/trauma team → TRAUMA CENTER (spread reds across trauma-capable hospitals)
     → Major burns → burn-capable center (if time allows; else stabilize at nearest)
     → Child → pediatric-capable hospital if time cost acceptable
  → YELLOW → hospitals with capacity, often further from scene
  → GREEN → bus/van with medic to hospital/clinic with spare capacity (NOT the closest)
  → Always: check capacity via Med Comms, log it

references: CDC 'In a Moment's Notice: Surge Capacity for Terrorist Bombings' (first-hour rule of thumb)
